SequencesAlgorithmsCounting
Game: People stand in a circle and, going round from the top, every few people one is removed until only one is left. Win by standing in the place of the last one.
How to play: Press a smiley to choose where you stand, then press Slow or Fast and watch who goes. Press Reset to try another place.
How many Every which
Look for the math

The historian Josephus Flavius, trapped in a cave with 40 soldiers, is said to have found the one place in the circle that survives when every third person is killed. This is the Josephus problem.

A recurrence

Number the places from 0 at the top. Let J(m) be the place that survives among m people when every k-th is removed. With one person, J(1) = 0. After the first removal, m − 1 people are left and the counting begins again k places further on, so J(m) = (J(m − 1) + k) mod m. The logic test compared this with the applet's own counting and with a plain list count, for every number of people from 3 to 50 and every k from 1 to 50 (2,400 games), and found the same survivor and the same order of removals every time.

Every second person

For k = 2 there is a neat closed form: write n = 2m + L with 0 ≤ L < 2m; counting from 1 at the top the survivor is place 2L + 1. With 50 people, 50 = 32 + 18, so place 37. The test checked this for every n up to 50. (Concrete Mathematics, by Graham, Knuth and Patashnik, treats the problem in full.)

The legend

With 41 people (Josephus and a friend) and every third killed, the last two are places 31 and 16 (counting from 1 at the top): the places the story says Josephus and his friend took. With 40 people, the page's number, the safe place is the one shown by the test.

As in the applet, the count starts at the top place (“1” is said there), so the first person to go is the k-th place from the top; the last person counted is the survivor and is not removed; and when your place is removed the game ends there.

Choose every 2nd with 16 people, then 17, then 31, then 32. Which places are safe, and can you see the pattern?
